translationRepairs: The emperor praised his integrity and raised Feng's rank to grand coachman of the imperial household.
The emperor praised his integrity and raised Feng's rank to Grandee of Splendid Light.
Chinese 光祿大夫 is Grandee of Splendid Light; “grand coachman of the imperial household” mistranslates a different office (太僕), and the proposed replacement is accurate.
The emperor praised his integrity and added Feng's rank to grand coachman of the imperial household.
The emperor praised his integrity and increased Feng's rank to that of Grandee of Splendid Light.
光祿大夫 is Grandee of Splendid Light, not Grand Coachman; 加秩 here increases Feng's rank to that grade.

Your Majesty did not measure your subject's ability yet appointed him metropolitan governor; he has had no way to prove himself, and you again raised your subject to grand coachman—office is lofty and responsibility heavy; it is not what your subject should hold.

Your Majesty did not measure your subject's ability yet appointed him metropolitan governor; he has had no way to prove himself, and you again raised your subject to Grandee of Splendid Light—office is lofty and responsibility heavy; it is not what your subject should hold.
復秩臣為光祿大夫 requires Grandee of Splendid Light, not grand coachman; keep the original em dash and wording around “office,” changing only the mistranslated title.
Fu Shang was the grand empress's half-brother and the nearest kin left.
Fu Shang, Palace Attendant and Grandee of Splendid Light, was the Imperial Great Empress Dowager's paternal cousin. She had raised him from childhood, and no bond was closer.
父同產子 means the son of a full sibling of her father, making Fu Shang her paternal cousin rather than her uncle or half-brother. 小自保大 says she raised him from childhood.
The emperor's uncle Wang Li used Li Shang of Nanyang to grab hundreds of qing of marsh and wasteland, then asked the court to pay for it.

At the time, the emperor's maternal uncle Wang Li, Marquis of Hongyang, had retainers use Nan Commandery Administrator Li Shang's influence to claim several hundred qing of uncultivated land. Much of it was marshland that the Privy Treasurer had leased to commoners and that they had already reclaimed. Wang Li then memorialized offering it to the government.
南郡 is Nan Commandery, not Nanyang. The fuller revision also preserves the commoners' prior leases and reclamation, which the draft omitted.

At that time the emperor's maternal uncle, Marquis of Hongyang Wang Li, had retainers acting through Administrator of Nanyang Li Shang seize several hundred qing of reclaimed grassland. Much of it was hillside and marsh that common people had leased from the Privy Treasurer—all was roughly developed—and they memorialized, wishing to turn it over to the commandery treasury.

At that time the emperor's maternal uncle, Marquis of Hongyang Wang Li, had retainers use the influence of Li Shang, Administrator of Nan Commandery, to claim several hundred qing of uncultivated land. Much of it consisted of marshland the Privy Treasurer had leased to commoners, nearly all of which had already been reclaimed. Wang Li memorialized, wishing to transfer it to the government.
南郡 must be Nan Commandery. The revision also clarifies the retainers' use of Li Shang, the commoners' leases, and 略皆開發.
Du Zhiji died the next winter.
Du Zhiji died the next year.
明年 means the next year; “next winter” invents a season absent from 明年，稚季病死.
Later Guangwudi honored the family with a post for his grandson Kang.
During the Jianwu era, when the court honored ministers of former merit, Bao's grandson Kang was appointed magistrate of Zhu.
The sentence names only the Jianwu era, not Guangwudi. 諸 is Zhu County in Langya and 長 is its magistrate, not a generic chief.
It scolded him for haggling with the Fu palace over slave prices.
Long ranks among the Nine Ministers, yet instead of correcting the court's failings, he memorializes to haggle with Yongxin Palace over the price of slave-girls, airing the dispute before everyone.
The original omits the edict's charge and invents 'Fu palace' for 永信宮. The revision restores Yongxin Palace and condenses the public wrangling into natural English.

When Emperor Ai died and Wang Mang took control of the government, he had Grand Minister of Works Kong Guang memorialize that Long, formerly Shepherd of Ji Province, had handled the Zhongshan Empress Dowager Feng case unjustly and trapped the innocent, and therefore should not hold office in the central region.

When Emperor Ai died and Wang Mang took control of the government, he had Grand Minister over the Masses Kong Guang memorialize that, as former Shepherd of Ji Province, Long had mishandled the case of Empress Dowager Feng of Zhongshan and entrapped innocent people, and therefore should not serve in the central government.
大司徒 is Grand Minister over the Masses, not Grand Minister of Works. 中朝 here is the central government, not a geographical region.

When Emperor Ai died, Wang Mang seized government and had Grand Minister of Works Kong Guang memorialize that Long, as former shepherd of Ji Province, had handled the Zhongshan Lady Feng case unjustly and trapped the innocent—he should not hold office in the central plain.

When Emperor Ai died, Wang Mang seized control of the government and had Grand Minister over the Masses Kong Guang memorialize that, as former Shepherd of Ji Province, Long had handled the case of Empress Dowager Feng of Zhongshan unjustly and entrapped innocent people; he therefore should not hold office in the central government.
The literal likewise requires Grand Minister over the Masses for 大司徒, and 中朝 means the central government rather than the central plain.
He Bing's grandfather relocated to Pingling on a clerk's salary.
He Bing, courtesy name Zilian, came from a family whose grandfather had moved from Pingyu to Pingling as a two-thousand-picul official.
The sentence gives He Bing's courtesy name and his grandfather's move from Pingyu. The revision retains both facts without the draft's awkward 'was a man whose' construction.
He was transferred to governor of Yingchuan, replacing Yan Xu of Lingsyang.
He was transferred to governor of Yingchuan, replacing Yan Xu of Lingyang.
陵陽 is Lingyang; “Lingsyang” is a spelling error with no support in the Chinese place name.
Later Guangwudi honored a grandson with a gentleman appointment.
During the Jianwu era, one of He Bing's grandsons was appointed a Gentleman.
The Chinese names only the Jianwu era and identifies the appointee as He Bing's grandson; it does not name Guangwudi.
Chengdi did adopt the Dingtao prince; Long won Ji Province and Yingchuan.
The emperor eventually established the King of Dingtao as crown prince; Long was promoted to Shepherd of Ji Province and Administrator of Yingchuan.
立定陶王為太子 records the king's establishment as crown prince, while 隆遷 introduces two offices to which Long was promoted.
Ai made him metropolitan governor, then Bearer of the Mace.
When Emperor Ai took the throne, Long entered the capital as Metropolitan Governor on the strength of his top performance rating, then was promoted to Bearer of the Mace.
The replacement restores the accession context, Long as the subject, and 以高第 as the basis for his appointment.
Eunuchs hauled ten wagonloads of arsenal weapons to Dong Xian and the nurse Wang.

At the time, Dong Xian, a Gentleman Attendant, was rising in favor. The emperor ordered palace eunuchs to draw weapons from the imperial arsenal in ten successive deliveries and send them to Dong Xian and the household of the emperor's wet nurse, Wang A.
前後十輩 describes ten successive deliveries or groups, not wagonloads; the replacement also restores both occurrences of Dong Xian and Wang A's name.
The privy purse feeds the harem, not the granary budget.
Even the emperor's own maintenance is not paid from the Grand Minister of Agriculture's funds; all expenditures for his support and rewards for service come from the Privy Treasurer.
The sentence expressly separates the Grand Minister of Agriculture's public funds from maintenance and rewards paid by the Privy Treasurer.
Keeping granary coin off petty spending was how Han drew the line between palace and state.

This ensures that essential reserves are not spent on incidental uses and the people's labor is not consumed by frivolous expenses; it distinguishes public from private and makes the proper course clear.
The replacement retains both prohibitions, including the omitted protection of the people's labor, and the stated public-private distinction.
He traced how axes and arsenal issues were tied to real military duty.

In antiquity, feudal lords and regional commanders empowered to wage punitive campaigns were granted axes and halberds. Han frontier officers charged with repelling raiders likewise receive weapons from the imperial arsenal; in every case, they receive them only after accepting the corresponding duty.
The Chinese gives Long's full analogy between campaign authority, frontier duty, and grants of state weapons; a one-line meta-summary does not translate it.
The Spring and Autumn canon forbade private armor to clip ministerial muscle.
According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals, private households may not store armor; this restrains the power of ministers and diminishes their private strength.
The revision translates the explicit ban on private armor and its purpose without the draft's modern slang.
He said giving state arms to Dong Xian and a nurse turned public gear into private toys.

Now Dong Xian and the others are merely fawning favorites and insignificant women favored in private, yet the empire's public resources supply their private households, and the state's instruments of military authority equip their families.
The source contrasts public resources and state weapons with favored private households; 'private toys' is unsupported and erases the memorial's direct argument.
He warned that arming playthings would teach the realm contempt.

The people's labor is diverted to favorites, and weapons of war are furnished to insignificant women. This arrangement is improper: it encourages arrogance and usurpation and sets the wrong example for the realm.
The replacement restores the diverted labor, furnished weapons, and explicit warning about arrogance and usurpation.
He quoted Confucius on the three Huan arsenals.
Confucius said, 'What place has this in the halls of the Three Families?'
The Chinese is a direct Confucius quotation about the halls of the Three Families; the draft's Huan arsenals are not present.
Confucius said, 'What can be taken from the hall of the three families!
Confucius said, 'What place has this in the halls of the Three Families?'
The literal requires a complete English question for 奚取於 and a closed quotation.
Your subject begs to collect the weapons back into the arsenal."
I ask that the weapons be recovered and returned to the arsenal."
收還武庫 asks that the issued weapons be recovered and returned to the arsenal.
Grand Dowager Fu's buyers underpaid palace women and skimmed Bearer of the Mace maids.
Before long, Empress Dowager Fu had attendants buy slave women from various government offices at cut-rate prices; she also took eight slave women from the office of the Bearer of the Mace.
傅太后 is Empress Dowager Fu, and the sentence distinguishes discounted purchases from the additional taking of eight women from Long's office.
Wujiang Long demanded fair prices for the sales.
Long memorialized that the price was too low and requested that a fair value be set.
奏言 and 請 describe a memorial reporting the low price and requesting fair revaluation, not an unspecified demand.
The edict called the quarrel vulgar and demoralizing."
His actions do not accord with right principle. From this comes his reputation for wrangling over advantage; he provides no example to the hundred officials and damages moral instruction and custom."
The edict explicitly alleges improper conduct, contentious grasping, a bad official example, and damage to moral instruction and custom.

He impeached the heir of General of the Guards Zhang Anshi—Pengzu, gentleman attendant at court and marquis of Yangdu—for failing to dismount at the palace hall gate, and linked the charge to Anshi's occupying office without real benefit.

He impeached the son of General of the Guards Zhang Anshi—Pengzu, gentleman attendant at court and marquis of Yangdu—for failing to dismount at the palace hall gate, and linked the charge to Anshi's occupying office without real benefit.
張安世子 names Pengzu as Anshi's son; 子 is not a designated heir.
The marquis of Wei laughed and said, "Cigong is mad while sober—what need of wine?"
The chancellor, the Marquis of Wei, laughed and said, "Cigong is mad while sober—what need of wine?"
丞相魏侯 names both the chancellorship and the Wei marquisate; the original drops 丞相, but Chancellor Marquis of Wei is awkward English.
He thanked the emperor for a letter from Master of Reading Yao: the censor must praise good and punish evil, not seize every case.
He thanked the emperor for a letter from Master of Writing Yao: the censor must praise good and punish evil, not seize every case.
尚書令堯 is a master of writing, not of reading.

I only fear there will be no cloud-bank of help, that I will be thrust aside by a crowd of wicked men, letting slanderers succeed, blocking the road of the straight, disheartening loyal ministers and sealing wise men's mouths—this is what your foolish subject fears."

I only fear there will be no help even in the least, that I will be thrust aside by a crowd of wicked men, letting slanderers succeed, blocking the road of the straight, disheartening loyal ministers and sealing wise men's mouths—this is what your foolish subject fears."
未有雲補 means not even the slightest remedy or help; 雲 is not a bank of clouds.
Even Wu and Zhou trembled at small omens, he argued—how much more should a childless age fear heaven's warnings.
Formerly King Wu and the Duke of Zhou, even after receiving the fish-and-crow omens, still trembled and warned one another—how much more should a childless age fear heaven's warnings.
武王、周公 are King Wu and the Duke of Zhou, and 魚烏之瑞 are auspicious omens they had already received, not fused Wu and Zhou trembling at small omens.

Thereupon Left General Xin Qingji, Right General Lian Bao, Chamberlain for Ceremonies Shi Dan, and Palace Grandee Gu Yong jointly submitted a memorial saying, "We have heard that an enlightened king extends a tolerant hearing, honors the offices of remonstrance and dispute, opens wide the path for loyal and upright men, and does not punish reckless or uncompromising words. Only then can the hundred officials in office exhaust their loyalty and offer all their plans without fearing later disaster; the court has no flatterers, and the sovereign has no guides who would lead him from the Way.

Thereupon Left General Xin Qingji, Right General Lian Bao, Chamberlain for the Palace Garrison Shi Dan, and Palace Grandee Gu Yong jointly submitted a memorial saying, "We have heard that an enlightened king extends a tolerant hearing, honors the offices of remonstrance and dispute, opens wide the path for loyal and upright men, and does not punish reckless or uncompromising words. Only then can the hundred officials in office exhaust their loyalty and offer all their plans without fearing later disaster; the court has no flatterers, and the sovereign has no guides who would lead him from the Way.
光祿勳 is the palace-garrison chamberlain, not Chamberlain for Ceremonies (太常).

Thereupon Left General Xin Qingji, Right General Lian Bao, Chamberlain for Ceremonies Shi Dan, and Grandee of the Palace Gu Yong jointly submitted a memorial saying, "We have heard that an enlightened king extends a tolerant ear, honors remonstrance officers, opens wide the road of loyalty and uprightness, and does not punish wild or blunt words—then the hundred officials hold their posts, exhaust loyalty and counsel, fear no later disaster, the court has no flatterers, and the sovereign has no guide who would lead him to lose the Way.

Thereupon Left General Xin Qingji, Right General Lian Bao, Chamberlain for the Palace Garrison Shi Dan, and Grandee of the Palace Gu Yong jointly submitted a memorial saying, "We have heard that an enlightened king extends a tolerant ear, honors remonstrance officers, opens wide the road of loyalty and uprightness, and does not punish wild or blunt words—then the hundred officials hold their posts, exhaust loyalty and counsel, fear no later disaster, the court has no flatterers, and the sovereign has no guide who would lead him to lose the Way.
The same 光祿勳 title is not the ceremonial chamberlaincy.
One was the Zhao empress's father—
The Marquis of Kongxiang is the empress's father;
孔鄉侯，皇后父 names the Marquis of Kongxiang as the empress's father and does not mention a Zhao empress.
Ai recalled him to censor, then metropolitan governor.
When Emperor Ai ascended the throne, Bao was summoned as Grandee Remonstrant and promoted to Colonel Director of the Retainers.
諫大夫 is grandee remonstrant and 司隸 is the retainers' commandant, not a Jingzhao metropolitan governor.
Sun Bao sent a chancellor's investigator, exposed the fraud, and impeached Li and Shang for deceiving the throne.
Sun Bao sent a chancellor's investigator, exposed the fraud, and impeached Wang Li and Li Shang for deceiving the throne.
立、尚 are Wang Li of Hongyang and administrator Li Shang; Li and Shang wrongly gives Wang Li the surname Li.

Li was not punished, but later when his elder brother Shang, Grand Marshal and General of the Guards, died, Li should have succeeded him next; the emperor passed over Li and appointed his younger brother Gen, Marquis of Quyang, Grand Marshal and Cavalry General.

Wang Li was not punished, but later when his elder brother Shang, Grand Marshal and General of the Guards, died, Wang Li should have succeeded him next; the emperor passed over Wang Li and appointed his younger brother Gen, Marquis of Quyang, Grand Marshal and Cavalry General.
立雖不坐 continues Wang Li after 尚下獄死; bare Li would confuse him with Li Shang.

When the memorial was submitted, the Son of Heaven was displeased. Because Bao was a noted minister, he could not bear to execute him, and therefore issued a formal edict to the chancellor and Grand Minister of Works: "Metropolitan Commandant Bao has memorialized that the former Vice Director of the Masters of Writing Chong was wronged, and asks that Master of Writing Zhao Chang be imprisoned and tried.

When the memorial was submitted, the Son of Heaven was displeased. Because Bao was a noted minister, he could not bear to execute him, and therefore issued a formal edict to the chancellor and Grand Minister of Works: "Metropolitan Commandant Bao has memorialized that the former Vice Director of the Masters of Writing Chong was wronged, and asks that Master of Writing Chang be imprisoned and tried.
尚書令昌 does not supply the surname Zhao, so that addition should drop; 司隸寶 is already well rendered as Metropolitan Commandant, and Director of Retainers is only a style swap.

It happened that Yuegui commandery reported a yellow dragon swimming in the river; Grand Tutor Kong Guang, grand minister of works Ma Gong, and others all praised Wang Mang's merit and virtue as comparable to the Duke of Zhou and said it should be announced at the ancestral temple.

It happened that Yuegui commandery reported a yellow dragon swimming in the river; Grand Preceptor Kong Guang, Grand Minister of Education Ma Gong, and others all praised Wang Mang's merit and virtue as comparable to the Duke of Zhou and said it should be announced at the ancestral temple.
大司徒 is Grand Minister of Education, not Works (大司空); the proposal still renders 太師 as Grand Tutor, which is 太傅.
Wang Mang recalled him to greet the boy emperor.
When Emperor Ai died, Wang Mang reported to Queen Mother Wang and summoned Bao as Grandee of the Palace to welcome the King of Zhongshan together with Wang Shun and others.
哀帝崩…白王太后徵寶以為光祿大夫，與王舜等俱迎中山王 names Ai's death, the queen mother, the appointment, Wang Shun, and the King of Zhongshan; boy emperor is invented.
Grand Minister of Agriculture funds are not taken from the imperial carriage for allowances; allowances and gifts for support all come from the privy treasury.
Even the imperial establishment is not supplied for its maintenance from Grand Minister of Agriculture funds; maintenance and rewards for service all come from the Privy Treasurer.
大司農錢自乘輿不以給共養 means even the emperor's keep is not paid from Da Sinong funds; the original reverses the source and the beneficiary.
Mang cashiered Shi Li, Ding Xuan, and Zhao Chang to Hepu.

Shi Li was then Palace Grand Coachman, Ding Xuan administrator of Taishan, and Zhao Chang—the Prefect of the Masters of Writing who had slandered Zheng Chong—administrator of Henei; all were dismissed from office and relocated to Hepu.
The sentence lists Shi Li, Ding Xuan, and Zhao Chang with offices and Zheng Chong, then 皆免官，徙合浦; it does not make Mang the subject.
Chengdi's mother wept to Ai for Wang Linqing.
The empress dowager of Emperor Cheng, because the Empress Dowager of Qiongcheng loved Linqing, wept when she heard of it and spoke to Emperor Ai.
成帝太后 weeps and speaks to Ai because 邛成太后愛林卿; the original drops that cause and the hearing.
He took Yingchuan from the mild magistrate Yan Xu.
He was transferred to governor of Yingchuan, replacing Yan Xu of Lingyang.
徙穎川太守，代陵陽嚴詡 is a transfer replacing Yan Xu of Lingyang; 陵陽 is a place-name, not mild, and 代 is succession, not seizure.
